nrem-sleep.short: Non-rapid-eye-movement sleep: the three stages N1 to N3, from light to deep. Brain waves slow down as sleep deepens.

rem-sleep.short: Rapid-eye-movement sleep: the stage with fast eye movements, low muscle tone and most dreaming. It alternates with NREM sleep through the night.

slow-wave-sleep.short: The deepest NREM stage (N3), named for its slow, large brain waves. It is the hardest stage to be woken from.

sleep-cycle.short: One loop through the sleep stages, about 90 minutes long. A night holds about 4 to 6 of them.

sleep-pressure.short: The urge to sleep that builds the longer you stay awake and falls during sleep. Adenosine is one driver.

circadian-rhythm.short: The body's inner clock of about 24 hours. It sets when you feel alert or sleepy, whatever your sleep debt.

chronotype.short: Your natural lean towards mornings (a lark) or evenings (an owl), set by your body clock.

sleep-deprivation.short: Going without any sleep for a night or more.

sleep-restriction.short: Sleeping less than you need, for example 4 to 5 hours in bed, for one night or more.

glucose-tolerance.short: How well the body clears sugar from the blood after a meal. Lower tolerance means blood sugar stays high for longer.

polysomnography.short: The reference way to measure sleep: sensors record brain waves, eye movements and muscle activity overnight, usually in a lab.

actigraphy.short: Estimating sleep from movement with a wrist-worn sensor. It is cheap and works at home, but it can mistake lying still for sleep.

sleep-efficiency.short: Time asleep divided by time in bed, as a percentage. 90% means 9 of every 10 minutes in bed were spent asleep.

sleep-extension.short: Spending more time in bed than usual, on purpose, for days or weeks, to raise total sleep.

sleep-hygiene.short: Habits and bedroom conditions that support sleep, such as regular sleep times, a dark cool room and no late caffeine.

sleep-inertia.short: The groggy, slowed state in the first minutes after waking, including after a nap.
